newsitem.title: THAILAND: Private group urges Thais to cut spending.
newsitem.headline: Private group urges Thais to cut spending.

text.p: An economic lobbying group said on Monday that the Thai government's strategy for reviving weak exports and stemming the economy's deterioration must be accompanied by a halt in wasteful consumer spending.

The Thai Economic Survival Lobby Group (TESLG), comprising more than 300 finance executives, businessmen and economists, said tackling a wide current-account deficit through export drives alone would not succeed.

"We must build a common awareness among Thais that they each can help in preventing the country from slipping into bankruptcy," said group member Apichart Intaravisit, assistant vice president of National Finance and Securities Plc.
Apichart urged wealthy Thais to cut back on foreign shopping trips and told government officials to reduce costly study tours abroad.

The group's members include Pin Chakkaphak, chief executive of Finance One Plc, Narong Pattamasaevi, president of Nithipat Capital Plc, Kovit Poshyananda, chairman of the Stock Exchange of Thailand, and Thanadee Soponsiri, president of Nava Finance and Securities Plc.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan has projected the 1996 current-account deficit will be a six-year high of 8.2 percent of gross domestic product, up from 8.1 percent in 1995. But he said the 1997 deficit would narrow to between 7.5 and 7.9 percent.

The Thai economy, hurt by zero growth in exports for 1996, is expected to expand by its lowest rate in a decade -- 6.7 percent -- this year against 8.6 percent in 1995. The government projects 7.0-7.5 percent growth in the next few years.
Poor economic indicators have dragged the Thai stock market down to a 51-month low this month, forcing out investors.

Phasuk Pongpaichitr, economist at Chulalongkorn University, described an economic action plan unveiled by Amnuay last week as lacking specific details on how to boost Thailand's ailing exports and industries.
"He did not touch export structural problems and was not convincing that he would really be able to trim military budgets," she said.

She added that although Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh had tried to appease the public by pledging to delay military spending, military leaders did not show a willingness to postpone committed arms acquisition plans.
"I think the finance minister is not strong enough to resist lobbies and business politics," she said.
The group warned in a statement issued over the weekend that Thailand would face national bankruptcy if Thais ignored the country's protracted current-account deficit.

"We are concerned that the financial and economic health of the country is in danger. The aggravating current-account deficit in the past few years has contributed to over 2.2 trillion baht ($87 billion) of foreign debt."
It said Thais annually spent over 80 billion baht on foreign holiday trips, 10 billion baht on sending children to study abroad, and seven billion baht on foreign luxuries.
"If we can persuade holiday makers to spend 10,000 baht less on each trip or to change cars every five years instead of two, things would be a lot better," Apichart said.
TESLG planned to gather 10,000 signatures in the next three to five months to further its campaign, he added.
